## Detail

### 01-unindexed-foreign-key

**Unindexed foreign key** — order_items has a foreign key to orders but no index on it, so every lookup of one order's lines reads the whole child table.

[Scenario notes and SQL](sql/scenarios/01-unindexed-foreign-key/) · naive **7.08 ms** → optimized **0.38 ms** (**18.7x**, 39 rows, verified identical)

|  | Median | Min | Max | Buffers (8 kB pages) | Indexes used |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| naive | 7.08 ms | 7.06 ms | 7.12 ms | 7,175 | `orders_customer_placed_idx` |
| optimized | 0.38 ms | 0.35 ms | 0.44 ms | 635 | `orders_customer_placed_idx`, `order_items_order_covering_idx` |

Objects the fix creates:

| Object | Kind | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `order_items_order_covering_idx` | index | 7.1 MB |

<details>
<summary>Plans</summary>

Naive:

```sql
-- Every line of every order placed by one customer, rolled up per order.
-- This is the shape of an "order history" page: a handful of orders, a few
-- lines each. It should touch a few dozen rows.
SELECT oi.order_id,
       sum(oi.quantity)   AS units,
       sum(oi.line_total) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.customer_id = 137
GROUP BY oi.order_id
ORDER BY oi.order_id
```

```text
Aggregate  (rows=39 actual=34.181ms buffers=1783)
  -> Sort  (rows=77 actual=34.145ms buffers=1783 sort=quicksort)
    -> Hash Join  (rows=77 actual=34.120ms buffers=1783)
      -> Seq Scan on order_items  (rows=183333 actual=15.892ms buffers=1743)
      -> Hash  (rows=39 actual=0.045ms buffers=40)
        -> Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (rows=39 actual=0.032ms buffers=40)
          -> Bitmap Index Scan using orders_customer_placed_idx  (rows=39 actual=0.005ms buffers=3)
Planning Time: 0.064 ms
Execution Time: 34.223 ms
```

Optimized:

```sql
-- Byte-for-byte the same query as naive.sql, on purpose.
--
-- The query was never the problem. What changed is that order_items now has an
-- index on the foreign key column, with the two aggregated columns carried in
-- the index payload, so the whole thing is answered without touching the heap.
SELECT oi.order_id,
       sum(oi.quantity)   AS units,
       sum(oi.line_total) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.customer_id = 137
GROUP BY oi.order_id
ORDER BY oi.order_id
```

```text
Aggregate  (rows=39 actual=0.140ms buffers=158)
  -> Sort  (rows=77 actual=0.110ms buffers=158 sort=quicksort)
    -> Nested Loop  (rows=77 actual=0.087ms buffers=158)
      -> Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (rows=39 actual=0.021ms buffers=40)
        -> Bitmap Index Scan using orders_customer_placed_idx  (rows=39 actual=0.004ms buffers=3)
      -> Index Only Scan using order_items_order_covering_idx on order_items  (rows=1.97 loops=39 actual=0.001ms buffers=118 heap_fetches=0)
Planning Time: 0.061 ms
Execution Time: 0.151 ms
```

</details>

### 02-deep-offset-pagination

**Deep OFFSET pagination** — OFFSET 40000 makes the server produce and discard 40000 rows before returning the 25 anybody wanted.

[Scenario notes and SQL](sql/scenarios/02-deep-offset-pagination/) · naive **8.32 ms** → optimized **0.25 ms** (**33.6x**, 25 rows, verified identical)

|  | Median | Min | Max | Buffers (8 kB pages) | Indexes used |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| naive | 8.32 ms | 8.04 ms | 8.58 ms | 80,286 | `orders_placed_at_id_idx` |
| optimized | 0.25 ms | 0.22 ms | 0.32 ms | 56 | `orders_placed_at_id_idx` |

Objects the fix creates:

| Object | Kind | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `orders_placed_at_id_idx` | index | 3.0 MB |

<details>
<summary>Plans</summary>

Naive:

```sql
-- One page of an order list, 25 rows, deep into the sequence.
--
-- The index below can produce the rows in exactly this order, so there is no
-- sort. It still has to walk :deep_offset index entries and fetch that many
-- heap tuples before it reaches the ones being asked for, and then throw all of
-- them away.
SELECT id, customer_id, status, placed_at, total_amount
FROM orders
ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
OFFSET 40000
LIMIT 25
```

```text
Limit  (rows=25 actual=14.197ms buffers=40143)
  -> Index Scan using orders_placed_at_id_idx on orders  (rows=40025 actual=11.058ms buffers=40143)
Planning Time: 0.017 ms
Execution Time: 14.204 ms
```

Optimized:

```sql
-- The same page, addressed by where the last page ended instead of by how many
-- rows precede it.
--
-- The row-wise comparison (placed_at, id) < (cursor, cursor) is not the same as
-- placed_at <= cursor AND id < cursor: it is a single lexicographic comparison,
-- and PostgreSQL can turn it directly into a starting position in a
-- two-column index. The scan begins at the answer.
SELECT id, customer_id, status, placed_at, total_amount
FROM orders
WHERE (placed_at, id) < (TIMESTAMPTZ '2025-09-05T04:40:51.000Z', 26699)
ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 25
```

```text
Limit  (rows=25 actual=0.016ms buffers=28)
  -> Index Scan using orders_placed_at_id_idx on orders  (rows=25 actual=0.012ms buffers=28)
Planning Time: 0.017 ms
Execution Time: 0.022 ms
```

</details>

### 03-correlated-subquery-to-window

**Correlated subquery per row** — Two correlated aggregates re-scan each customer's order history once per order, turning a linear job into a quadratic one.

[Scenario notes and SQL](sql/scenarios/03-correlated-subquery-to-window/) · naive **229 ms** → optimized **10.1 ms** (**22.7x**, 2161 rows, verified identical)

|  | Median | Min | Max | Buffers (8 kB pages) | Indexes used |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| naive | 229 ms | 227 ms | 232 ms | 1,864,535 | `orders_customer_placed_idx` |
| optimized | 10.1 ms | 10.0 ms | 10.5 ms | 4,062 | `orders_customer_placed_idx` |

<details>
<summary>Plans</summary>

Naive:

```sql
-- For each order of a few heavy accounts: which number it is in that
-- customer's history, and the running total spent up to and including it.
--
-- Each output row triggers two correlated aggregates, and each of those
-- re-reads that customer's order history from the beginning. A customer with
-- 700 orders costs 700 * 700 index entries, twice.
SELECT o.id,
       o.customer_id,
       o.placed_at,
       o.total_amount,
       (SELECT count(*)
          FROM orders o2
         WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id
           AND o2.placed_at <= o.placed_at)          AS order_seq,
       (SELECT sum(o3.total_amount)
          FROM orders o3
         WHERE o3.customer_id = o.customer_id
           AND o3.placed_at <= o.placed_at)          AS running_total
FROM orders o
WHERE o.customer_id BETWEEN 2 AND 6
ORDER BY o.customer_id, o.placed_at, o.id
```

```text
Sort  (rows=2161 actual=373.600ms buffers=464282 sort=quicksort)
  -> Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (rows=2161 actual=372.596ms buffers=464282)
    -> Bitmap Index Scan using orders_customer_placed_idx  (rows=2161 actual=0.104ms buffers=18)
    -> SubPlan 1: Aggregate  (rows=1 loops=2161 actual=0.052ms buffers=9412)
      -> Index Only Scan using orders_customer_placed_idx on orders  (rows=237.5 loops=2161 actual=0.031ms buffers=9412 heap_fetches=0)
    -> SubPlan 2: Aggregate  (rows=1 loops=2161 actual=0.119ms buffers=453859)
      -> Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (rows=237.5 loops=2161 actual=0.084ms buffers=453859)
        -> Bitmap Index Scan using orders_customer_placed_idx  (rows=237.5 loops=2161 actual=0.012ms buffers=9411)
Planning Time: 0.157 ms
Execution Time: 373.779 ms
```

Optimized:

```sql
-- The same two numbers, computed in a single ordered pass per customer.
--
-- The default frame for a window with ORDER BY is
-- RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which includes every peer
-- row with the same placed_at. That is exactly what "placed_at <= o.placed_at"
-- means in the naive version, so the answers match even where timestamps tie.
-- Writing ROWS instead of RANGE here would silently change the answer.
SELECT o.id,
       o.customer_id,
       o.placed_at,
       o.total_amount,
       count(*)             OVER w AS order_seq,
       sum(o.total_amount)  OVER w AS running_total
FROM orders o
WHERE o.customer_id BETWEEN 2 AND 6
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY o.customer_id ORDER BY o.placed_at)
ORDER BY o.customer_id, o.placed_at, o.id
```

```text
Incremental Sort  (rows=2161 actual=3.689ms buffers=1011)
  -> WindowAgg  (rows=2161 actual=3.131ms buffers=1011)
    -> Sort  (rows=2161 actual=1.714ms buffers=1011 sort=quicksort)
      -> Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (rows=2161 actual=0.876ms buffers=1011)
        -> Bitmap Index Scan using orders_customer_placed_idx  (rows=2161 actual=0.108ms buffers=18)
Planning Time: 0.087 ms
Execution Time: 3.860 ms
```

</details>

### 04-top-n-per-group-lateral

**Top-N per group over the whole table** — Ranking every order in the table to return the three most recent for a few hundred customers.

[Scenario notes and SQL](sql/scenarios/04-top-n-per-group-lateral/) · naive **49.2 ms** → optimized **3.95 ms** (**12.5x**, 781 rows, verified identical)

|  | Median | Min | Max | Buffers (8 kB pages) | Indexes used |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| naive | 49.2 ms | 48.8 ms | 50.7 ms | 11,485 | `customers_pkey` |
| optimized | 3.95 ms | 3.81 ms | 4.04 ms | 14,463 | `customers_pkey`, `orders_customer_placed_idx` |

<details>
<summary>Plans</summary>

Naive:

```sql
-- The three most recent orders of each customer in a small cohort.
--
-- row_number() is computed over every order in the table, because the window
-- has to be complete before the rn <= 3 filter can be applied. All 100,000
-- orders are sorted to answer a question about a few hundred customers.
SELECT c.id AS customer_id,
       c.email,
       r.id AS order_id,
       r.placed_at,
       r.total_amount,
       r.rn
FROM customers c
JOIN (
    SELECT o.id,
           o.customer_id,
           o.placed_at,
           o.total_amount,
           row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY o.customer_id
                              ORDER BY o.placed_at DESC, o.id DESC) AS rn
    FROM orders o
) r ON r.customer_id = c.id AND r.rn <= 3
WHERE c.id BETWEEN 15000 AND 15400
ORDER BY c.id, r.rn
```

```text
Incremental Sort  (rows=781 actual=81.479ms buffers=2301)
  -> Merge Join  (rows=781 actual=81.273ms buffers=2301)
    -> WindowAgg  (rows=38652 actual=77.816ms buffers=2291)
      -> Sort  (rows=90516 actual=56.519ms buffers=2291 sort=external merge)
        -> Seq Scan on orders  (rows=100000 actual=13.541ms buffers=2291)
    -> Index Scan using customers_pkey on customers  (rows=401 actual=0.086ms buffers=10)
Planning Time: 0.159 ms
Execution Time: 81.601 ms
```

Optimized:

```sql
-- The same three rows per customer, fetched one customer at a time.
--
-- LATERAL lets a subquery in the FROM clause reference the row to its left, so
-- each iteration is an ordered index range scan that stops after three rows.
-- The work is proportional to the number of customers asked about, not to the
-- size of the orders table.
SELECT c.id AS customer_id,
       c.email,
       r.id AS order_id,
       r.placed_at,
       r.total_amount,
       row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY c.id
                          ORDER BY r.placed_at DESC, r.id DESC) AS rn
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT o.id, o.placed_at, o.total_amount
    FROM orders o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
    ORDER BY o.placed_at DESC, o.id DESC
    LIMIT 3
) r
WHERE c.id BETWEEN 15000 AND 15400
ORDER BY c.id, rn
```

```text
Incremental Sort  (rows=781 actual=2.181ms buffers=2069)
  -> WindowAgg  (rows=781 actual=1.946ms buffers=2069)
    -> Incremental Sort  (rows=781 actual=1.654ms buffers=2069)
      -> Nested Loop  (rows=781 actual=1.452ms buffers=2069)
        -> Index Scan using customers_pkey on customers  (rows=401 actual=0.069ms buffers=10)
        -> Limit  (rows=1.95 loops=401 actual=0.003ms buffers=2059)
          -> Incremental Sort  (rows=1.95 loops=401 actual=0.002ms buffers=2059)
            -> Index Scan using orders_customer_placed_idx on orders  (rows=2.14 loops=401 actual=0.001ms buffers=2059)
Planning Time: 0.052 ms
Execution Time: 2.251 ms
```

</details>

```text
Planning Time: 0.025 ms
```

```text
Sort  (rows=6 actual=1.479ms buffers=98 sort=quicksort)
```

### 06-or-across-tables

**OR across two tables** — An OR whose arms live on different tables cannot be answered by either table's index, so the join has to be materialised in full.

[Scenario notes and SQL](sql/scenarios/06-or-across-tables/) · naive **19.2 ms** → optimized **3.24 ms** (**5.9x**, 850 rows, verified identical)

|  | Median | Min | Max | Buffers (8 kB pages) | Indexes used |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| naive | 19.2 ms | 19.1 ms | 19.5 ms | 7,837 | — |
| optimized | 3.24 ms | 3.15 ms | 3.40 ms | 3,225 | `orders_status_idx`, `customers_email_uq`, `orders_customer_placed_idx` |

Objects the fix creates:

| Object | Kind | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `orders_status_idx` | index | 696 kB |

<details>
<summary>Plans</summary>

Naive:

```sql
-- Every refunded order from the last quarter, plus every order at all from one
-- specific customer.
--
-- Both arms of the OR are individually indexable: orders.status has an index
-- (setup.sql), customers.email has a unique one. Neither can be used, because a
-- row qualifies if EITHER is true, and the two live on different tables. The
-- planner's only option is to join everything and filter afterwards.
SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.status, o.placed_at, o.total_amount
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE (o.status = 'refunded' AND o.placed_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2025-10-01 00:00:00+00')
   OR c.email = 'customer137@example.com'
ORDER BY o.id
```

```text
Sort  (rows=850 actual=36.688ms buffers=2532 sort=quicksort)
  -> Hash Join  (rows=850 actual=36.434ms buffers=2532)
    -> Seq Scan on orders  (rows=100000 actual=9.342ms buffers=2291)
    -> Hash  (rows=20000 actual=4.958ms buffers=241)
      -> Seq Scan on customers  (rows=20000 actual=2.261ms buffers=241)
Planning Time: 0.085 ms
Execution Time: 36.764 ms
```

Optimized:

```sql
-- One indexable query per arm, concatenated.
--
-- UNION ALL rather than UNION: UNION would sort and deduplicate the whole
-- result, which can cost more than the scan just eliminated. The second arm
-- instead excludes what the first arm already returned, so there is nothing to
-- deduplicate. Note that the exclusion is the negation of the WHOLE first arm,
-- not just of its status test -- getting that wrong is how this rewrite starts
-- returning duplicate rows.
--
-- The join to customers is dropped from the first arm because it was a no-op:
-- orders.customer_id is a NOT NULL foreign key to customers.id, so the inner
-- join matches exactly one row and cannot change the result.
SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.status, o.placed_at, o.total_amount
FROM orders o
WHERE o.status = 'refunded'
  AND o.placed_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2025-10-01 00:00:00+00'

UNION ALL

SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.status, o.placed_at, o.total_amount
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.email = 'customer137@example.com'
  AND NOT (o.status = 'refunded'
           AND o.placed_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2025-10-01 00:00:00+00')

ORDER BY id
```

```text
Sort  (rows=850 actual=0.914ms buffers=1058 sort=quicksort)
  -> Append  (rows=850 actual=0.700ms buffers=1058)
    -> Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (rows=811 actual=0.547ms buffers=1014 filtered=1611)
      -> Bitmap Index Scan using orders_status_idx  (rows=2422 actual=0.055ms buffers=4)
    -> Nested Loop  (rows=39 actual=0.028ms buffers=44)
      -> Index Scan using customers_email_uq on customers  (rows=1 actual=0.002ms buffers=4)
      -> Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (rows=39 actual=0.017ms buffers=40)
        -> Bitmap Index Scan using orders_customer_placed_idx  (rows=39 actual=0.003ms buffers=3)
Planning Time: 0.097 ms
Execution Time: 0.986 ms
```

</details>

### 07-distinct-to-semi-join

**DISTINCT hiding a fan-out join** — A join to a child table produces tens of thousands of duplicate wide rows, and DISTINCT throws almost all of them away.

[Scenario notes and SQL](sql/scenarios/07-distinct-to-semi-join/) · naive **21.9 ms** → optimized **2.97 ms** (**7.4x**, 614 rows, verified identical)

|  | Median | Min | Max | Buffers (8 kB pages) | Indexes used |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| naive | 21.9 ms | 21.9 ms | 22.0 ms | 7,522 | `customers_loyalty_tier_idx`, `events_customer_id_idx` |
| optimized | 2.97 ms | 2.95 ms | 3.11 ms | 5,570 | `customers_loyalty_tier_idx`, `events_customer_id_idx` |

Objects the fix creates:

| Object | Kind | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `customers_loyalty_tier_idx` | index | 152 kB |
| `events_customer_id_idx` | index | 2.4 MB |

<details>
<summary>Plans</summary>

Naive:

```sql
-- Full customer record for every platinum member who appears in the event log.
--
-- The join to events is there only to answer "does a row exist". Because it is
-- a join, it produces one output row per matching event -- around a hundred per
-- customer -- and DISTINCT then collapses them back down. Almost all of the
-- work is spent building rows that are immediately discarded.
SELECT DISTINCT
       c.id,
       c.email,
       c.full_name,
       c.country,
       c.loyalty_tier,
       c.is_active,
       c.created_at
FROM customers c
JOIN events e ON e.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.loyalty_tier = 'platinum'
ORDER BY c.id
```

```text
Sort  (rows=614 actual=42.755ms buffers=1880 sort=quicksort)
  -> Aggregate  (rows=614 actual=42.568ms buffers=1880)
    -> Nested Loop  (rows=74684 actual=21.959ms buffers=1880)
      -> Bitmap Heap Scan on customers  (rows=614 actual=0.097ms buffers=13)
        -> Bitmap Index Scan using customers_loyalty_tier_idx  (rows=614 actual=0.009ms buffers=2)
      -> Index Only Scan using events_customer_id_idx on events  (rows=121.64 loops=614 actual=0.014ms buffers=1867 heap_fetches=0)
Planning Time: 0.116 ms
Execution Time: 42.818 ms
```

Optimized:

```sql
-- The same question asked as a question.
--
-- EXISTS is a semi-join: the executor stops probing as soon as it finds one
-- matching event, and the customer row is emitted once. There is nothing to
-- deduplicate because nothing was duplicated.
SELECT c.id,
       c.email,
       c.full_name,
       c.country,
       c.loyalty_tier,
       c.is_active,
       c.created_at
FROM customers c
WHERE c.loyalty_tier = 'platinum'
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM events e WHERE e.customer_id = c.id)
ORDER BY c.id
```

```text
Sort  (rows=614 actual=0.935ms buffers=1856 sort=quicksort)
  -> Nested Loop  (rows=614 actual=0.780ms buffers=1856)
    -> Bitmap Heap Scan on customers  (rows=614 actual=0.083ms buffers=13)
      -> Bitmap Index Scan using customers_loyalty_tier_idx  (rows=614 actual=0.008ms buffers=2)
    -> Index Only Scan using events_customer_id_idx on events  (rows=1 loops=614 actual=0.001ms buffers=1843 heap_fetches=0)
Planning Time: 0.068 ms
Execution Time: 0.986 ms
```

</details>

```sql

-- dashboard, run again on every page load, by every user, all day.

       count(DISTINCT o.id)           AS orders,
       sum(oi.line_total)             AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id

ORDER BY 1
```

### 11-sort-limit-index

**Sort and limit over a large table** — A top-50 list sorts 100k rows because no index provides the requested ordering, including the tiebreaker's direction.

[Scenario notes and SQL](sql/scenarios/11-sort-limit-index/) · naive **21.7 ms** → optimized **0.30 ms** (**72.5x**, 50 rows, verified identical)

|  | Median | Min | Max | Buffers (8 kB pages) | Indexes used |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| naive | 21.7 ms | 21.1 ms | 24.4 ms | 6,873 | — |
| optimized | 0.30 ms | 0.29 ms | 0.31 ms | 106 | `orders_total_amount_idx` |

Objects the fix creates:

| Object | Kind | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `orders_total_amount_idx` | index | 3.0 MB |

| ordering | plan_shape |
| --- | --- |
| total_amount DESC, id ASC | Limit <- Index Only Scan using orders_total_amount_idx on orders |
| total_amount DESC, id DESC | Limit <- Index Only Scan Backward using orders_total_amount_plain_tmp on orders |
| total_amount ASC, id ASC | Limit <- Index Only Scan using orders_total_amount_plain_tmp on orders |

<details>
<summary>Plans</summary>

Naive:

```sql
-- The fifty largest orders.
--
-- Note the mixed sort directions: descending by amount, ascending by id. That
-- is a deliberate tiebreaker choice -- oldest order first among equal amounts --
-- and it is what makes this scenario about index *direction* rather than just
-- index presence.
SELECT id, customer_id, status, placed_at, total_amount
FROM orders
ORDER BY total_amount DESC, id ASC
LIMIT 50
```

```text
Limit  (rows=50 actual=36.254ms buffers=2291)
  -> Sort  (rows=50 actual=36.244ms buffers=2291 sort=top-N heapsort)
    -> Seq Scan on orders  (rows=100000 actual=13.608ms buffers=2291)
Planning Time: 0.056 ms
Execution Time: 36.274 ms
```

Optimized:

```sql
-- Identical query. The index created by setup.sql matches the ordering exactly,
-- so the sort disappears entirely and the scan stops after fifty rows.
SELECT id, customer_id, status, placed_at, total_amount
FROM orders
ORDER BY total_amount DESC, id ASC
LIMIT 50
```

```text
Limit  (rows=50 actual=0.025ms buffers=53)
  -> Index Scan using orders_total_amount_idx on orders  (rows=50 actual=0.017ms buffers=53)
Planning Time: 0.012 ms
Execution Time: 0.032 ms
```

</details>

| `products_search_gin` | index | 1.3 MB |

<details>
<summary>Plans</summary>

Naive:

```sql
-- Search the catalogue.
--
-- to_tsvector() is evaluated for every row: concatenate, tokenise, stem,
-- discard stop words, build a sorted lexeme vector -- 20,000 times, to return a
-- handful of products.
SELECT id, sku, name
FROM products
WHERE to_tsvector('english', name || ' ' || coalesce(description, ''))
      @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'titanium thermos')
ORDER BY id
```


Optimized:

```sql
-- expression the naive query recomputes, and is covered by a GIN index.

FROM products
WHERE search_vector @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'titanium thermos')
ORDER BY id
```

```text
Sort  (rows=68 actual=0.084ms buffers=72 sort=quicksort)
  -> Bitmap Heap Scan on products  (rows=68 actual=0.069ms buffers=72)
```
